title: Amos 2:6–16
context: The oracles reach their climax as the LORD turns to Israel. He charges them with selling the righteous and the needy, trampling the poor, sexual exploitation that profanes his name, and worship conducted on garments taken in pledge. He recalls his grace in destroying the Amorite, bringing them out of Egypt, and raising up prophets and Nazirites, whom Israel silenced and corrupted. Judgment will leave the swift, the strong, and the brave unable to escape. Shared ground: both traditions read the passage as a call to covenant accountability, justice for the poor, and respect for God’s messengers.

verses.text: The LORD says: “For three transgressions of Israel, yes, for four, I will not turn away its punishment, because they have sold the righteous for silver, and the needy for a pair of sandals;
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD says Israel will be punished because “they have sold the righteous for silver, and the needy for a pair of sandals.” The climax falls on Israel.

Arminian readers see injustice against the poor condemned.
verses.reformedNotes:
The phrase may refer to debt slavery for trivial sums, though the exact practice is debated.

Reformed readers see covenant violation in oppression. Shared ground: God defends the poor.

verses.text: They trample the heads of the poor into the dust of the earth and deny justice to the oppressed. A man and his father use the same maiden, to profane my holy name.
verses.arminianNotes:
They trample the poor into the dust and deny justice to the oppressed; a man and his father use the same young woman, profaning God’s holy name.

Arminian readers see social and moral corruption joined.
verses.reformedNotes:
Whether the young woman is a servant exploited by the household or someone connected to a shrine is debated; the text is best read soberly.

Reformed readers agree. Shared ground: exploitation profanes God’s name.

verses.text: They lay themselves down beside every altar on clothes taken in pledge. In the house of their God they drink the wine of those who have been fined.
verses.arminianNotes:
They lie beside every altar on garments taken in pledge and drink wine of those who were fined in the house of their God. Worship and exploitation mix.

Arminian readers see religion used to cover injustice.
verses.reformedNotes:
The law required pledged garments to be returned before sunset (Exodus 22:26–27; Deuteronomy 24:12–13).

Reformed readers see worship emptied by oppression. Shared ground: God rejects worship that profits from injustice.

verses.text: Yet I destroyed the Amorite before them, whose height was like the height of the cedars, and he was strong as the oaks; yet I destroyed his fruit from above, and his roots from beneath.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD recalls destroying the Amorite, tall as cedars and strong as oaks, root and fruit, before Israel. Past grace is remembered.

Arminian readers see God’s gifts as a reason for gratitude and faithful response.
verses.reformedNotes:
The image of a tree destroyed from fruit to roots pictures complete removal.

Reformed readers see God’s sovereign grace in Israel’s history. Shared ground: both traditions read this as God reminding Israel that the land was his gift, which deepens their accountability.

verses.text: Also I brought you up out of the land of Egypt and led you forty years in the wilderness, to possess the land of the Amorite.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD brought them up from Egypt and led them forty years in the wilderness to possess the Amorite’s land. The exodus is recalled.

Arminian readers see covenant history inviting a faithful response from those who benefited.
verses.reformedNotes:
The shift to direct address (“I brought you up”) makes the history personal.

Reformed readers see God’s grace as the foundation of the covenant. Shared ground: both traditions read this as God’s saving acts forming the basis of Israel’s obligation to justice.

verses.text: I raised up some of your sons for prophets, and some of your young men for Nazirites. Isn’t this true, you children of Israel?” says the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD raised up some of their sons as prophets and some young men as Nazirites, asking, “Isn’t this true, you children of Israel?”

Arminian readers see God’s gifts of guidance and devotion.
verses.reformedNotes:
The rhetorical question invites Israel to admit God’s goodness.

Reformed readers see God providing faithful witnesses. Shared ground: both traditions read this as God’s continuing gifts to Israel, which made their later resistance more serious.

verses.text: “But you gave the Nazirites wine to drink, and commanded the prophets, saying, ‘Don’t prophesy!’
verses.arminianNotes:
“But you gave the Nazirites wine to drink, and commanded the prophets, saying, ‘Don’t prophesy!’” Israel resisted God’s gifts.

Arminian readers see a deliberate refusal of the guidance and devotion God had provided.
verses.reformedNotes:
Nazirites vowed to avoid wine (Numbers 6:3), and Amaziah later tells Amos not to prophesy at Bethel (7:13).

Reformed readers see hostility to God’s word. Shared ground: silencing God’s messengers is a grave covenant breach.

verses.text: Behold, I will crush you in your place, as a cart crushes that is full of grain.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD will crush them in their place as a cart full of grain crushes. Judgment is pictured vividly.

Arminian readers see the weight of judgment answering the weight of the injustice already named.
verses.reformedNotes:
The image may picture something pressed down under a heavy load; the precise sense is debated.

Reformed readers see God’s judgment as certain. Shared ground: both traditions read this as a vivid picture of the coming judgment on Israel, with the details of the image held loosely.

verses.text: Flight will perish from the swift. The strong won’t strengthen his force. The mighty won’t deliver himself.
verses.arminianNotes:
Flight will fail the swift, the strong will not strengthen his force, and the mighty will not deliver himself. Human strength fails.

Arminian readers see that no natural ability can escape God’s judgment.
verses.reformedNotes:
The list of failed abilities stresses the impossibility of escape.

Reformed readers see God overcoming every human resource. Shared ground: both traditions read this as a warning against trusting in one’s own strength when God has declared judgment.

verses.text: He who handles the bow won’t stand. He who is swift of foot won’t escape. He who rides the horse won’t deliver himself.
verses.arminianNotes:
The archer will not stand, the swift will not escape, and the horseman will not deliver himself. The list continues.

Arminian readers see every kind of military skill rendered useless before God’s judgment.
verses.reformedNotes:
The repetition builds a sense of complete defeat.

Reformed readers see the futility of human power against God. Shared ground: both traditions read this as a sober picture of judgment from which neither skill nor speed provides an escape.

verses.text: He who is courageous among the mighty will flee away naked on that day,” says the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes:
Even the bravest of the mighty will flee naked on that day, says the LORD. The oracle ends with shame.

Arminian readers see pride brought low and confidence in human courage exposed as empty.
verses.reformedNotes:
Fleeing naked pictures abandoning everything in panic.

Reformed readers see God humbling the strong. Shared ground: both traditions read this as the climax of the oracles, where Israel, which may have welcomed judgment on its neighbors, finds itself judged as well.
